clue.text: Fair amount? Strike!

definitions.meaning: a fair ... is British slang for a reasonable share or a sizeable amount
to hit someone hard, to wallop them

explanation.surface: Someone haggling over a fair share, then calling a walkout.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are the same word: a share or portion in slang, and a heavy blow as a verb.

clue.text: Opposed in two ways, party hit back before elected

indicators.note: in tells us the next pieces go inside the pair of street abbreviations
two asks for the ways abbreviation to be written twice over

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

indicators.note: before places the song ahead of the word for elected
hit back is read as the party song written backwards

parts.note: Agadoo was a 1984 party song by Black Lace, a staple of discos and weddings
IN means elected, as a candidate who gets in

explanation.surface: A politician resisting on two fronts after their party lashed out ahead of winning.
explanation.walkthrough: The party hit is 'Agadoo', a cheesy 1984 disco singalong by Black Lace; 'back' turns it round. 'two' doubles the street abbreviation, and 'in' sets the rest between that pair.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand against something is to resist it, and also to run as a rival candidate, hence the clue's two ways.

clue.text: Not entirely luxurious benefit

indicators.note: not entirely means the word for luxurious loses its final letter

parts.note: plush means luxurious, as in a plush hotel

explanation.surface: A perk that is only partly lavish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely' drops the last letter, H, from PLUSH.
explanation.definitionFit: A plus is an advantage or benefit, as in 'the garden is a real plus'.

clue.text: Political institution dispensing with French leader from afar, Marine Le Pen up to no good

indicators.note: no good means the letters are in a bad state, so they are to be rearranged
dispensing with tells us a letter is to be thrown out of the following word
from names the word, afar, that the letter is taken out of
the leader of French is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Marine Le Pen, the French far-right leader, stirring up mischief from a distance against a political body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dispensing with ... from' removes F (French leader) from AFAR, leaving AAR; 'no good' rearranges AAR with MARINELEPENUPTO.
explanation.definitionFit: The European Parliament is the elected legislative body of the European Union, a political institution.

clue.text: Arenas in development finally breaking down, perfect when up

indicators.note: breaking says the down word is split open by the final letter

parts.note: down means sad, low in spirits

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of development
in a down clue, up means the word for perfect is read from bottom to top

parts.note: A1 means first-rate or perfect, written here as AI

explanation.surface: Sports venues still being built, with a final collapse after a perfect start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' puts T (development's last letter) into SAD to give STAD; 'when up' turns A1 (top quality, the 1 written as I) into IA.
explanation.definitionFit: Stadia is the classical plural of stadium, and stadiums are sporting arenas.

clue.text: Huge beasts once beating toads in battle

indicators.note: in tells us the scrambled toads sit inside the battle

parts.note: Mons is the Belgian town that gave its name to the 1914 Battle of Mons

indicators.note: beating means the toads are battered into a new shape, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Prehistoric giants trampling amphibians in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beating' rearranges TOADS to ASTOD, which goes 'in' MONS (the First World War battle in Belgium).
explanation.definitionFit: Mastodons were huge elephant-like mammals that died out thousands of years ago, so beasts of old.

clue.text: Number of connected rooms in silhouette?

indicators.note: in, with the question mark, hints that the answer is present in the word silhouette, but with its letters in a different order

explanation.surface: A puzzle about how many rooms connect, judged from an outline.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of SILHOUETTE rearrange exactly; the question mark warns that 'in' is a loose signal that the answer lies, jumbled, within that word.
explanation.definitionFit: A suite is a set of linked rooms in a hotel, and each one has its own room number.

clue.text: Instrument in need of tuning, first off

indicators.note: first off means the opening letter is removed

parts.note: a note that is sharp is too high, so the instrument needs tuning

explanation.surface: A musician noticing their instrument is out of tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first off' drops the S from SHARP.
explanation.definitionFit: The harp is a stringed musical instrument plucked with the fingers.

clue.text: Average place to host a tapeworm, say?

indicators.note: to host means the words for average and place together hold the letter a inside

parts.note: par is the standard or average level, as in 'below par'
a site is a place

explanation.surface: An ordinary spot where a tapeworm might settle in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to host' puts the letter between the golfing term for average and the word for place, splitting the pair rather than one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tapeworm is an example of an organism that lives off a host, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Large cushions started to go in the middle — a lot!

indicators.note: to go in the middle means the central letter of the word for started is removed

parts.note: began means started
bags means a lot, as in 'bags of time'

explanation.surface: Someone flopping onto big cushions with plenty of enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go in the middle' removes G, the middle letter of BEGAN; BAGS for 'a lot' is British informal, as in 'bags of room'.
explanation.definitionFit: Beanbags are large floppy cushions filled with beads that are used as seats.

clue.text: Odd bits of carbon, sulphur, steel and cement, possibly, for me?

indicators.note: odd bits are the first, third and fifth letters of carbon

parts.note: S is the chemical symbol for sulphur
steel is a poetic word for a sword
cement is an example of something that sets hard, a setter

explanation.surface: A list of building materials and chemicals, then a puzzled question about who they are for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'me' is the person who wrote the clue, so the definition is the clue's author speaking. 'Odd bits of' takes CRO from carbon.
explanation.definitionFit: The setter of a puzzle often refers to themselves as me, so the word stands for its compiler.

clue.text: English invading, Ned has front limbs equipped for battle? You must be prepared!

indicators.note: invading means the English letter pushes into the phrase for battle

parts.note: war is battle
Ned's can be short for Ned has or Ned is, so this gives NED and IS
fore means front, as in the fore part of a ship
armed literally means equipped with arms, the upper limbs, as well as carrying weapons

explanation.surface: Ned, his forelimbs ready for a fight, while the English invade: a warning to be ready.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invading' slots the English letter into 'for battle'. 'Ned has' is read as Ned's, a contraction that can also stand for Ned is.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says knowing of danger in advance lets you get ready, so it is advice to be prepared.

clue.text: Those known by experts to hold sanctimonious views

indicators.note: to hold means the first word surrounds the second

parts.note: an expert is said to know their onions
pi is informal for pious or sanctimonious

explanation.surface: Specialists who are said to cling to self-righteous beliefs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Know your onions' is a British idiom for being an expert, so experts know ONIONS; PI is short for pious.
explanation.definitionFit: Opinions are views held by someone, as in 'what are your views on this'.

clue.text: Eternal youth has to fade — savage!

parts.note: to peter out is to fade away gradually
to pan is to criticise harshly, to savage a show

explanation.surface: A young person who must fade, followed by a brutal critique.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Barrie's character is the boy who never grows up, a byword for perpetual boyhood.

clue.text: See 12
No one annoyed about wear and tear

indicators.note: about tells us the whole run of pieces is turned round

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
sore means annoyed, as in feeling sore about it

explanation.surface: Nobody is irritated by everyday damage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns NOISORE round, back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Erosion is gradual wearing away, the slow damage that use or weather causes.

clue.text: See 2
Male leaving a horrible drink for Roman statesman

indicators.note: leaving means the male letter goes out of the next word

parts.note: grim means horrible
cola is a fizzy drink

explanation.surface: A man walking away from a nasty drink served to an ancient Roman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' takes M (male) out of GRIM to give GRI.
explanation.definitionFit: Agricola was a Roman general and governor of Britain, the father-in-law of the historian Tacitus.

clue.text: Still fashion designs about right for formal wear

parts.note: even means still, as in 'even more'

indicators.note: about means the reshaped letters go around the right letter
fashion as a verb means to shape, so the letters of designs are reshaped

explanation.surface: Quiet fashion designs, roughly right for a formal occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashion' rearranges DESIGNS into INGDESS, and 'about' wraps that round R to make INGDRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Evening dress is the formal clothing worn to dinners and balls, such as a gown or dinner jacket.

clue.text: Get lost somewhere in India on the road

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: Goa is a state on India's west coast
a way is a road, as in Appian Way

explanation.surface: Losing your bearings while travelling through India.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are blunt commands telling someone to leave you alone.

clue.text: Rise in temperature believable

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the words temperature believable

explanation.surface: A credible report of a fever going up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise' looks like a noun describing the temperature but is a verb, as in rising up against rulers.
explanation.definitionFit: To rise up against authority is to revolt, the act of a mutineer or insurgent.

clue.text: Time to fill bottles, say

indicators.note: bottles means holds inside, so the word for fill encloses the time letter

parts.note: to sate is to fill up or satisfy

explanation.surface: It is the moment to fill some bottles, perhaps at a winery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottles' is a verb: SATE holds T inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To state something is to declare or express it in words.

clue.text: Permission for a minor change of plan not as recent

indicators.note: a change of the following words means their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A teenager asking permission, after altering an out-of-date plan.
explanation.definitionFit: A child needs agreement from mother or father to do some things, such as a school trip.

clue.text: American's excellent in the opera Faust, all concluding

indicators.note: all concluding means take the final letter of each of the next words

explanation.surface: An American critic praising Gounod's opera Faust as it ends.
explanation.definitionFit: In American slang, neat means great or terrific, as in 'that's really neat'.

clue.text: Literary work losing focus for the present time

indicators.note: the focus of a word is its central letter, which is lost

parts.note: a novel is a work of literature

explanation.surface: A book that wanders off point, written for the here and now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing focus' removes V, the middle letter of NOVEL. 'The present time' is not 'now' but the season of gifts.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel means Christmas, the season when presents are given, a pun on present.

clue.text: See 4
